title: Everything Matters
author: Cheryl Swope
summary: Cheryl Swope, author of the Simply Classical curriculum for special learners, recounts an early special-education job in which a jaded psychiatrist told her, "In my experience, nothing matters anyway." She rejects that counsel of futility, drawing on her experience as a professional and as an adoptive parent of children with serious needs, and answers that everything matters. The habits of teaching, leisure and life form families and schools, so the choice between pop culture, hyper-individualized entertainment and screens on one side, and read-alouds, conversation, art, music and strong math instruction on the other, is consequential. She urges early attention to a child's difficulties without reducing the child to a list of disabilities, accommodations and goals, and asks educators to walk alongside rather than push children along a conveyor belt. She closes with forgiveness and perseverance, and a catalogue of everyday teaching acts that all matter.
points: Swope answers a psychiatrist's fatalism with a counter-claim that every choice in teaching, leisure and home life forms a child, so nothing is neutral.
She frames the formative choice as between screens and hyper-individualized entertainment and a diet of classic read-alouds, conversation, art, music and effective instruction.
Early intervention matters, but a child must never be reduced to diagnoses, accommodations and quantifiable goals.
She likens good special education to patient companionship rather than pushing students "forward" along an artificial conveyor belt.
The piece ends by naming perseverance and forgiveness, for parents as much as children, as the humane response to inevitable failures.
quotes: I did not believe the man’s words then, nor do I believe them now. As a professional but also as a parent I believe quite the opposite: Everything matters.
Then he added, as if to educate us with his counsel, “In my experience, nothing matters anyway.
Habits of teaching, leisure, and life form us as families and as schools.

How we view our children will inform our care of them. We must address a child’s difficulties early, rather than allow such difficulties to become entrenched and enlarged, but we must also remember to embrace and uphold our child’s humanity no matter his challenges.

We must resist reducing any child to merely a list of disabilities, accommodations, and quantifiable goals. Let us not simply push our children “forward” as if on an artificial conveyor belt, but rather let us wait patiently and walk alongside those who need our help, our dedication, and our companionship.
Weaker academic areas are targeted to build memory, concentration, and diligence. We seek to enrich and enlighten as we teach.

Every garden you grow together with your students, every great work of art you study, every mathematical problem you solve, every symphony you attend, every good book you read and every lesser book you dismiss, every angry temper you calm and fear you allay, every healing moment you share, and every kindness you give to the person before you—all of it matters.
